 What is driving the recent AI apocalypse warnings from tech CEOs and researchers? 

 Click here to take the poll and don't forget to share your thoughts in the WSB comments section . 
 
 
 
 
 
    
 
 
 
    
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Good morning! Here's the latest in trending: 

 Crude watch: Saudi pipeline outage and America to keep Iran's oil? 

 EU associate member: Canada is exploring closer ties across the pond. 

 $5K midterm dividend: Trump says the U.S. can 'easily' handle that .


 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Top News
 
 
 
 Scared money 
 
 
 
Getty Images
 
 
 The AI doomsday narrative has been making headlines, with more lab insiders raising red flags about the upcoming technology. Anthropic ( ANTHRO ) researcher Jacob Coxon recently resigned from the company, asserting that artificial intelligence could become powerful systems capable of causing human extinction by the end of the decade. Shortly thereafter, the claim was echoed by Evan Hubinger, Anthropic's Alignment Science Lead, who pegged the odds at over 10% while conceding that no laboratory currently has a plan in place to safely contain superintelligence.

 Executive alarm: Adding fuel to the fire have been leaders of the platforms themselves. AI-related stocks fell under pressure on Monday , with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei urging AI companies to "slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models." OpenAI ( OPENAI ) CEO Sam Altman also jumped on the bandwagon , agreeing that "we need to pace the frontier," while SpaceXAI's ( SPCX ) Elon Musk added that "Dario is right" and retweeted posts comparing AGI risks to nuclear weapons.

While there can be some very real risks here, like the Hugging Face attack , it's also important to note how existential risk narratives and doomsday framing have historically been used to mobilize money into emerging technology sectors. Threat-based urgency is not only effective in attracting investment, but routinely justifies unprecedented capital expenditures. Examples of this include Y2K and IT modernization in the 1990s, apocalyptic climate change and cleantech in the 2000s, and the imminent death of the financial system and crypto in the 2010s.

 Time is critical: Major AI players that have been pumping billions into AI companies and ventures have some big bills coming due soon, forcing them to raise even more cash absent immediate subscription profits or clear margin expansion. "The credit quality of hyperscalers is gradually weakening. Every time we take a deep dive into this sector, we find that capex is rising faster than we anticipated, financings are becoming more complicated and less transparent, and that returns on investment will take years to realize," S&P analysts led by Naveen Sarma wrote in a research note . "The stakes are high. We assume the top six U.S. hyperscalers will spend more than $7T on data centers and AI-related capex from 2025 through to 2030. The spending has been an increasingly important component of the U.S. economy and markets." ( 4 comments )
